concept.name: Chase-Lev Work-Stealing Deques & Fork-Join Schedulers

relationships.description: Shares cache-line padding and atomic memory-ordering mechanics with Chase-Lev deques.

concept.tagline: Scale multi-core task scheduling with lock-free LIFO owner deques, atomic CAS FIFO stealing, and zero-spin worker parking.
concept.purpose: Master Chase-Lev deque invariants, SeqCst memory fences, half-batch stealing, 61-tick fairness, and single-worker unparking.

spark.summary: Chase-Lev work-stealing deques let each core push/pop LIFO lock-free at the Bottom while idle cores steal FIFO from the Top via Atomic CAS.
spark.keyTakeaway: Keep 95%+ of task ops lock-free in local LIFO deques, pad top/bottom cache lines, and poll the global queue every 61 ticks for fairness.
spark.byteSummary:
When 16 or 64 CPU cores pull lightweight tasks or coroutines from a single mutex-protected global queue, every spawn and poll triggers cache-line ping-ponging across cores—burning more cycles fighting over the lock than running actual application code.

A **Chase-Lev Work-Stealing Deque** gives each worker thread its own local double-ended circular buffer. The **owner thread** pushes and pops tasks strictly at the **Bottom** in **LIFO** order—hitting warm L1/L2 cache lines with zero locks and no CAS on the common path. Whenever another worker runs out of local work, it becomes a thief and steals from the **Top** of a busy worker's deque in **FIFO** order using a single-word **Atomic Compare-And-Swap (CAS)**.

Stealing from the opposite end minimizes contention with the owner (who only contends with thieves when `size == 1`) and naturally steals the oldest, coarsest-grained fork-join subtrees. Production runtimes like Tokio, Go's `G-M-P` scheduler, and Java `ForkJoinPool` pair local deques with periodic global-queue fairness checks (`1/61`), randomized steal victims, and idle-core parking.

learningJourney.title: Why Global Mutex Queues Collapse & How Local Deques Scale
learningJourney.purpose: Contrast O(cores) global lock cache-line ping-ponging against lock-free per-worker Chase-Lev deques.

explanation.foundation: Assume 32 worker threads spawn millions of sub-microsecond tasks into one shared mutex queue. Every push and pop invalidates the lock's 64-byte cache line across all 32 cores, collapsing throughput.
explanation.core: A Chase-Lev deque assigns one local circular buffer per worker. The owner pushes and pops at the Bottom (LIFO) for hot L1 cache locality, while idle thieves steal from the Top (FIFO) via Atomic CAS.
explanation.deepDive: Because LIFO keeps newly spawned child tasks on the same core (still hot in L1/L2) and FIFO steals the oldest root-level tasks, work-stealing maximizes both cache hit rate and load balance.

learningJourney.title: Top/Bottom Indices, SeqCst Fence & Last-Item CAS Race
learningJourney.purpose: Trace the exact atomic memory ordering needed so an owner pop() and a thief steal() never both claim the last task.

explanation.foundation: Each deque maintains two monotonic 64-bit indices: `bottom` (written only by the owner) and `top` (updated via CAS by thieves and last-item owner pops).
explanation.core: On `pop()`, the owner decrements `b = bottom - 1` and executes a full **`SeqCst` memory fence** before reading `t = top`. Without that fence, CPU store-load reordering could let both owner and thief read stale indices and double-execute the last task!
explanation.deepDive: If `t == b` (last item), the owner races with thieves via `CAS(&top, t, t + 1)` and resets `bottom = t + 1` regardless of who won.

sectionDiagram.title: Top/Bottom Indices, SeqCst Fence & Last-Item CAS Race

cards.label: Why SeqCst Is Mandatory
cards.detail: On x86 TSO and ARM64, a store to bottom followed by a load of top can reorder without an explicit SeqCst fence.

cards.label: Steal Path
cards.detail: A thief reads top (Acquire), fence, reads bottom (Acquire); if t < b, reads slot and tries CAS(&top, t, t+1).

cards.label: 64-Byte Padding
cards.detail: Pad top and bottom onto separate 64-byte cache lines to avoid false sharing.

sectionDiagram.summary: A SeqCst fence between decrementing bottom and reading top prevents double-execution on the last-item CAS race.
sectionDiagram.caption: A SeqCst fence between decrementing bottom and reading top prevents double-execution on the last-item CAS race.

learningJourney.title: Bounded Power-of-2 Chase-Lev Deque with Overflow Spillover
learningJourney.purpose: Implement a power-of-2 masked work-stealing deque that spills excess tasks to a global queue instead of dropping.

explanation.foundation: Fixed-capacity local deques (e.g., 256 slots) avoid dynamic array resizing races and fit completely in L1/L2 cache.
explanation.core:
```python
class LocalWorkDeque:
    def __init__(self, cap_pow2: int = 256) -> None:
        if cap_pow2 <= 0 or (cap_pow2 & (cap_pow2 - 1)) != 0:
            raise ValueError('Capacity must be a positive power of 2')
        self.mask = cap_pow2 - 1
        self.ring = [None] * cap_pow2
        self.top = 0
        self.bottom = 0

    def push_or_spill(self, task, global_overflow: list) -> bool:
        if self.bottom - self.top > self.mask:
            # Spill half batch to global queue on local overflow
            global_overflow.append(task)
            return False
        self.ring[self.bottom & self.mask] = task
        self.bottom += 1
        return True
```
explanation.deepDive: When a local 256-slot ring fills up during a recursive fork storm, Go and Tokio spill half of the local queue to the global queue in one batch so idle cores immediately pick up the excess.

sectionDiagram.title: Bounded Power-of-2 Chase-Lev Deque with Overflow Spillover

cards.label: Bitmask Indexing
cards.detail: Power-of-2 capacity replaces slow integer division with a 1-cycle bitwise AND (bottom & mask).

cards.label: Zero Dynamic Resize Races
cards.detail: Fixed 256-slot rings eliminate the complex concurrent array-reallocation reclamation needed by unbounded deques.

cards.label: Batch Spillover
cards.detail: Spilling to the global queue on overflow acts as automatic load shedding to other cores.

sectionDiagram.summary: Fixed 256-slot bitmask rings with global overflow spillover eliminate array-resize races and balance bursts.
sectionDiagram.caption: Fixed 256-slot bitmask rings with global overflow spillover eliminate array-resize races and balance bursts.

learningJourney.title: Stealing Half-Batches & Randomized Victim Selection
learningJourney.purpose: Amortize steal CAS overhead by stealing half the victim's deque at once and randomizing victim order.

explanation.foundation: If 31 idle cores all check Worker 0 first in fixed order `[0, 1, 2...]`, they stampede Worker 0's `top` cache line.
explanation.core: Each thief picks a **randomized starting victim** (via per-thread `xorshift` PRNG) and steals **half** (`(b - t + 1) // 2`) of the victim's tasks in a single batch.
explanation.deepDive: Batch stealing cuts cross-core CAS traffic by ~10x during fork-join fan-outs and ensures newly woken thieves don't immediately starve.

sectionDiagram.title: Stealing Half-Batches & Randomized Victim Selection

cards.label: No Victim Stampede
cards.detail: Randomized coprime stride spreads 31 thieves evenly across all busy workers.

cards.label: Half-Batch Amortization
cards.detail: Stealing 128 tasks in 1 CAS gives the thief plenty of local work before its next cross-core steal.

cards.label: LIFO Fast Slot
cards.detail: Tokio also keeps a 1-item LIFO slot outside the deque so ping-ponging coroutines skip even local deque indexing.

sectionDiagram.summary: XorShift victim randomization and half-batch steals cut cross-core CAS contention by an order of magnitude.
sectionDiagram.caption: XorShift victim randomization and half-batch steals cut cross-core CAS contention by an order of magnitude.

learningJourney.title: Preventing Global-Queue Starvation & Blocking-Syscall Hijacks
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent LIFO fast-paths from starving global tasks and isolate blocking I/O onto dedicated thread pools.

explanation.foundation: Two classic bugs hit work-stealing runtimes: (1) two ping-ponging tasks keep the LIFO slot busy forever, starving the global queue; (2) a synchronous `fsync()` or DNS call blocks a worker thread.
explanation.core: Poll the global injection queue once every **61 local ticks** (`tick % 61 == 0`) to guarantee bounded wait times. Offload blocking syscalls via `spawn_blocking` or sysmon handoff (Go's `P` detachment).
explanation.deepDive: Enforce **cooperative preemption** (e.g., 128-poll budget per task slice) so tight CPU loops yield cleanly back to the deque.

sectionDiagram.title: Preventing Global-Queue Starvation & Blocking-Syscall Hijacks

cards.label: Prime Interval 61
cards.detail: Checking the global queue every 61st tick prevents lockstep synchronization across cores.

cards.label: Cooperative Budgeting
cards.detail: A task running >128 async polls yields to the back of the queue so other tasks make progress.

cards.label: Blocking Pool Offload
cards.detail: Never run synchronous disk/FFI calls on work-stealing worker threads.

sectionDiagram.summary: 61-tick global polling, 128-poll cooperative budgets, and blocking-pool offloading prevent starvation.
sectionDiagram.caption: 61-tick global polling, 128-poll cooperative budgets, and blocking-pool offloading prevent starvation.

learningJourney.title: Zero-CPU Idle Worker Parking & Thundering-Herd Wakeup Suppression
learningJourney.purpose: Park idle workers in epoll/futex without spinning 100% CPU while avoiding waking all 64 cores for 1 task.

explanation.foundation: Busy-spinning idle thieves burns 100% CPU and thermal-throttles active cores; waking all 64 parked cores for 1 spawned task wastes kernel futex cycles.
explanation.core: Track an atomic `num_searching` counter: cap active thieves at `cores / 2`, park excess idle workers on an `epoll`/`futex` condvar, and wake **at most 1** parked worker when a new task is spawned (only if `num_searching == 0`).
explanation.deepDive: If a woken worker finds work and sees more tasks remaining, it cascades by waking 1 additional parked peer.

sectionDiagram.title: Zero-CPU Idle Worker Parking & Thundering-Herd Wakeup Suppression

cards.label: Searching Cap
cards.detail: Limiting concurrent thieves to cores/2 prevents idle cores from saturating memory bandwidth.

cards.label: Single-Wakeup Invariant
cards.detail: Waking 1 worker when num_searching == 0 eliminates 64-thread thundering-herd futex storms.

cards.label: Zero-Spin Idle
cards.detail: Idle microservices drop to ~0% CPU usage cleanly.

sectionDiagram.summary: Capping concurrent thieves and waking 1 worker at a time eliminates idle spin and futex thundering herds.
sectionDiagram.caption: Capping concurrent thieves and waking 1 worker at a time eliminates idle spin and futex thundering herds.

learningJourney.title: Tracking Steal Ratios, Global-Queue Depth & Poll-Budget Preemptions
learningJourney.purpose: Instrument worker utilization, steal success rate, global spillover, and long-poll task stalls.

explanation.foundation: Invisible blocking calls inside async tasks silently halve runtime throughput without raising CPU metrics.
explanation.deepDive: Alert whenever `task_poll_duration_p99_us > 1,000 us` (indicating an accidental synchronous blocking call on a worker thread).

sectionDiagram.title: Tracking Steal Ratios, Global-Queue Depth & Poll-Budget Preemptions

cards.label: Blocking-Task Detector
cards.detail: A single poll() taking >1 ms flags synchronous mutexes or file I/O inside async code.

cards.label: Steal Efficiency
cards.detail: High failed-steal counts with low idle parking indicate steal-backoff tuning is needed.

cards.label: Overflow Surge Alert
cards.detail: Rising global_queue_depth signals tasks are spawning faster than cores can drain.

knowledgeChecks.question: In a Chase-Lev work-stealing deque, why does the owner push/pop from the **Bottom (LIFO)** while thieves steal from the **Top (FIFO)**?

options.text: LIFO keeps newly spawned child tasks hot in the owner's L1/L2 cache, while FIFO lets thieves grab the oldest, coarsest tasks with zero contention except when size == 1.
options.feedback: Correct! Opposite-end access maximizes cache locality and minimizes cross-core CAS contention.

options.text: Because CPUs only support Atomic CAS on even memory addresses.
options.feedback: Atomic CAS works on any aligned word; opposite ends minimize contention and optimize task granularity.

options.text: Because LIFO guarantees strict global FIFO fairness across all clients.
options.feedback: LIFO favors locality; global queue 61-tick polling handles fairness.

options.text: To force every push() to acquire a global mutex.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Owner LIFO at Bottom preserves cache warmth; thief FIFO at Top steals older coarse work with minimal contention.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is a `SeqCst` memory fence required in the owner's `pop()` between decrementing `bottom` and reading `top`?

options.text: To prevent CPU store-load reordering from letting both the owner and a concurrent thief read stale indices and double-execute the last task.
options.feedback: Correct! Without SeqCst, the store to bottom and load of top can reorder on x86/ARM.

options.text: To flush dirty pages from PostgreSQL to NVMe.
options.feedback: SeqCst is a CPU memory ordering fence, not a disk fsync.

options.text: To resize the circular buffer to 10,000 slots.
options.feedback: Bounded 256-slot deques do not resize dynamically.

options.text: To wake up all 64 parked worker threads.
options.feedback: Worker unparking uses futex/condvar signaling, not pop() fences.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Store-load reordering between bottom-- and reading top would break mutual exclusion on the last element without SeqCst.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why do runtimes like Tokio check the global injection queue periodically (e.g., every 61st tick) instead of only when local deques are empty?

options.text: To prevent two ping-ponging local tasks from monopolizing the LIFO slot and starving tasks waiting in the global queue indefinitely.
options.feedback: Correct! Periodic global-queue polling guarantees bounded fairness under heavy local task spawning.

options.text: Because local deques are deleted every 61 milliseconds.
options.feedback: Local deques persist for the lifetime of the worker.

options.text: Because epoll only returns events on prime-numbered ticks.
options.feedback: 61 is chosen as a prime tick interval for fairness, unrelated to epoll.
Work stealing remains active whenever a worker runs out of local work.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Periodic global polling bounds tail wait time when local tasks continuously re-spawn each other.

beginner.summary: Work-stealing gives each CPU core its own to-do list so cores don't fight over one lock, and idle cores borrow work from busy neighbors.
beginner.keyTakeaway: Workers grab newest tasks from their own list (warm cache) and steal oldest tasks from neighbors when idle.
beginner.byteSummary: If 32 workers share one to-do list, they spend all their time waiting in line for the lock. Giving each worker its own list—and letting idle workers quietly steal from the back of a busy neighbor's list—scales smoothly across all CPU cores.

intermediate.summary: Chase-Lev deques pair lock-free LIFO Bottom ops with SeqCst-fenced last-item CAS, 256-slot bitmask rings, and randomized half-batch stealing.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: Pad top/bottom onto separate 64-byte cache lines, spill overflows to a global queue, and poll global every 61 ticks.
